# Install Apps {.unnumbered} :::: {.callout-warning collapse='false' appearance='default' icon='false'} ## [Caution]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.25em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.00em; color: var(--callout-body-color, #282b2d);'} This section is being revised. Thank you for your patience. ::: :::: ## Finding your applications Installing an application and being able to *run* it are two different problems. A package manager like `yum` puts binaries somewhere the shell already knows to look, but anything I install by hand usually lands somewhere the shell doesn't check. That's when a command I know is installed comes back as `command not found`. ### The `PATH` variable `PATH` is an environment variable holding a colon separated list of directories. When I type a command, the shell walks that list from left to right and runs the first matching executable it finds. It never searches the whole filesystem. Print it to see what the shell is actually checking: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} echo $PATH ``` ::: ```{.default} /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/sbin:/home/ec2-user/.local/bin:/home/ec2-user/bin ``` To find out which copy wins, use `which`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} which python3 ``` ::: ```{.default} /usr/bin/python3 ``` If a command isn't found, the executable is almost always on the box, just not in one of those directories. Adding it is a matter of appending the directory to `PATH` in a startup file so the change survives a new login: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} echo 'export PATH="/opt/python/3.12.1/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc source ~/.bashrc ``` ::: Putting the new directory first means it takes priority over anything with the same name further down the list. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'How PATH Search Works' %%| fig-width: 8.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}}%% graph TD Cmd(["shell command
python3"]) --> Check1("Check
/usr/local/bin") Check1 -->|"not found"| Check2("Check
/usr/bin") Check2 -->|"found!"| Run("Run
/usr/bin/python3") Check1 -->|"found!"| Run2("Run
/usr/local/bin/python3
(first match wins)") style Cmd fill:#d2562b,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff style Check1 fill:#e8a33d,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 style Check2 fill:#e8a33d,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 style Run fill:#5b8c5a,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff style Run2 fill:#5b8c5a,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff ``` :::: {.callout-note collapse='true' appearance='default' icon='false'} ## [PATH is per user]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.15em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.00em; color: var(--callout-body-color, #282b2d);'} Editing `~/.bashrc` only changes `PATH` for that one account. A service running under `systemd` doesn't read it at all, and neither does a different user who logs in later. If an application has to be visible to everyone (and to services), a symlink into `/usr/local/bin` is more reliable than asking every account to edit a startup file. ::: :::: ### Symlinks with `ln` A symlink is a pointer: a small file that redirects to a real one somewhere else. Rather than adding a new directory to everyone's `PATH`, I create a link inside a directory that's already there. The `-s` flag makes it symbolic, and the real path always comes first: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo ln -s /opt/python/3.12.1/bin/python3.12 /usr/local/bin/python3 ``` ::: Confirm the link points where you expect: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} ls -l /usr/local/bin/python3 ``` ::: ```{.default} lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 33 Aug 21 14:02 /usr/local/bin/python3 -> /opt/python/3.12.1/bin/python3.12 ``` ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Symlink Resolution' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}}%% graph TD User["User types:
python3"] Link["/usr/local/bin/python3"] Points["/opt/python/3.12.1/
bin/python3.12"] Real["Actual binary"] User --"Shell finds symlink"--> Link Link --"Symlink points to"--> Points Points --"Real executable runs"--> Real style User fill:#d2562b,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff style Link fill:#2a6f77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style Points fill:#e8a33d,stroke:#000,stroke-width:1px,color:#000 style Real fill:#5b8c5a,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff ``` The other reason I reach for `ln` is versioning. When a new version of R or Python goes into `/opt` alongside the old one, repointing a single symlink switches every user over, and repointing it back is the rollback. ## Where do applications live? Linux spreads a single application across several directories by purpose, not by product. Knowing the convention is how I find a config file or a log without searching for it. | Location | What lives there | |:---------|:-----------------| | `/bin`, `/usr/bin` | Core system executables, managed by the package manager | | `/usr/local/bin` | Executables installed outside the package manager, plus symlinks | | `/opt` | Self contained third party software, one directory per version | | `/etc` | Configuration files | | `/var/log` | Log files | : Common application locations {#tbl-app-locations} ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Application Filesystem Hierarchy' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}}%% graph TD Root(["/"]) Bin("/bin or
/usr/bin") Local("/usr/local/bin") Opt("/opt") OptPy("/opt/python/3.12.1") OptR("/opt/R/4.6.1") Etc("/etc") Log("/var/log") Root --"OS managed"--> Bin Root --"symlinks here"--> Local Root --"versions isolated"--> Opt Root --"config files"--> Etc Root --"log files"--> Log Opt --"lib, bin, share"--> OptPy Opt --"lib, bin, share"--> OptR style Root fill:#d2562b,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff,font-size:12px,font-family:monospace style Bin fill:#2a6f77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff,font-size:12px,font-family:monospace style Local fill:#5b8c5a,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff,font-size:12px,font-family:monospace style Opt fill:#e8a33d,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px,color:#000,font-size:12px,font-family:monospace style OptPy fill:#e8a33d,stroke:#000,stroke-width:1px,color:#000,font-size:12px,font-family:monospace style OptR fill:#e8a33d,stroke:#000,stroke-width:1px,color:#000,font-size:12px,font-family:monospace style Etc fill:#666,stroke:#999,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff,font-size:12px,font-family:monospace style Log fill:#666,stroke:#999,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff,font-size:12px,font-family:monospace ``` `/opt` is the important one for data science work. Installing there keeps a version fully contained in its own folder, so nothing overwrites anything the operating system depends on. ## Language versions AWS EC2 instances will not have data science language installed (at least not versions we can use), so the instructions below cover how to install Python and R onto the EC2 instance we've SHH'd into ### Python version The Python already on the instance belongs to the operating system. Amazon Linux 2 uses it for `yum` and other internal tooling, so upgrading it or installing packages into it with `sudo pip install` risks breaking the box itself. The safer pattern is to install your own Python into `/opt`, leave the system copy alone, and create virtual environments from the `/opt` copy: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} /opt/python/3.12.1/bin/python3.12 -m venv ~/my-app/venv ``` ::: Activate the virtual environment: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} source ~/my-app/venv/bin/activate ``` ::: Deactivate the virtual environment with: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} deactivate ``` ::: ### R version R has no equivalent system dependency, so multiple versions can coexist in `/opt/R` without conflict. [`rig`](https://github.com/r-lib/rig), the R Installation Manager, handles installing and switching between them. `rig` isn't in the Amazon Linux 2 repositories, so install it first. The portable Linux build is a tarball that unpacks into `/usr/local`, which puts `rig` in `/usr/local/bin` and on the `PATH` for every account: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} curl -Ls https://github.com/r-lib/rig/releases/download/latest/rig-linux-x86_64-latest.tar.gz | \ sudo tar xz -C /usr/local rig --version ``` ::: On a Graviton (`arm64`) instance, swap `x86_64` for `aarch64` in the URL. With `rig` installed, add R and make it the default: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo rig add 4.6.1 ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo rig default 4.6.1 ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} rig list ``` ::: `rig` is one way to get R. On an Ubuntu machine (a local workstation, or an Ubuntu AMI instead of Amazon Linux), CRAN publishes its own `apt` repository, which tracks the current release (R 4.6.1 as of this writing). Add CRAN's signing key and repository, then install `r-base`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo apt update -qq ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo apt install --no-install-recommends software-properties-common dirmngr ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} wget -qO- https://cloud.r-project.org/bin/linux/ubuntu/marutter_pubkey.asc | \ sudo tee -a /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/cran_ubuntu_key.asc ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo add-apt-repository "deb https://cloud.r-project.org/bin/linux/ubuntu $(lsb_release -cs)-cran40/" ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo apt install --no-install-recommends r-base ``` ::: `$(lsb_release -cs)` fills in the Ubuntu release codename. Pop!_OS is built on Ubuntu and reports the Ubuntu codename (`noble` on Pop!_OS 24.04), so the same commands work unchanged. CRAN currently builds for 26.04 (`resolute`), 24.04 (`noble`), and 22.04 (`jammy`). Confirm the version: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} R --version | head -1 ``` ::: ```{.default} R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24) -- "Happy Hop" ``` This installs a single, system wide R under `/usr/lib/R` that `apt upgrade` keeps current. If you need several versions side by side, use `rig` instead; it works the same way on Ubuntu. `rig` answers "*which R is installed on this box?*" It doesn't pin the packages a project uses or the system libraries those packages compile against. [`rix`](https://docs.ropensci.org/rix/) covers that side. It writes a `default.nix` file describing a project's R version, R packages, and system dependencies, and [Nix](https://nixos.org/) builds that environment into `/nix/store`, isolated from both the system and anything `rig` installed. | Tool | Scope | Lives in | |:-----|:------|:---------| | `rig` | R versions for the whole instance | `/opt/R/` | | `rix` + Nix | R, packages, and system libraries for one project | `/nix/store`, described by `default.nix` | : rig versus rix {#tbl-rig-rix} Install Nix with the Determinate Systems installer, which the `rix` docs recommend. The extra configuration adds the `rstats-on-nix` binary cache, so R packages download prebuilt instead of compiling on the instance: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf -L https://install.determinate.systems/nix | \ sh -s -- install --no-confirm --extra-conf " trusted-users = root $USER substituters = https://cache.nixos.org https://rstats-on-nix.cachix.org trusted-public-keys = cache.nixos.org-1:6NCHdD59X431o0gWypbMrAURkbJ16ZPMQFGspcDShjY= rstats-on-nix.cachix.org-1:vdiiVgocg6WeJrODIqdprZRUrhi1JzhBnXv7aWI6+F0=" ``` ::: Open a new shell so `nix-shell` and `nix-build` are on your `PATH`. The R that `rig` installed can generate the environment file, so install `rix` into it and describe the project: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} mkdir -p ~/my-r-app && cd ~/my-r-app Rscript -e 'install.packages("rix", repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")' ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} Rscript -e ' rix::rix( r_ver = "4.6.1", r_pkgs = c("dplyr", "shiny"), system_pkgs = NULL, git_pkgs = NULL, ide = "none", project_path = ".", overwrite = TRUE )' ``` ::: `ide = "none"` fits a server with no editor attached. `rix()` writes `default.nix` and an `.Rprofile`; the `.Rprofile` keeps R inside the Nix environment from reading the library paths of the `rig` installed R. Build the environment, then enter it: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} nix-build nix-shell ``` ::: Inside `nix-shell`, `R` and `Rscript` resolve to the Nix copy, not `/opt/R`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} which R Rscript -e 'R.version.string' ``` ::: `which R` should print a path under `/nix/store`. `exit` leaves the shell and puts the `rig` default back in front. Commit `default.nix` with the project and anyone running `nix-build` gets the same R, packages, and system libraries, which also sidesteps the `-devel` packages below for anything Nix provides. ### System libraries Both languages depend on system libraries that neither one installs for you. A package that compiles from source will fail with a missing header error until the matching development package is present: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo yum install -y libcurl-devel openssl-devel libxml2-devel ``` ::: These are the three that account for most failed installs of `curl`, `openssl`, and `xml2`, and every R or Python package that depends on them. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Language Runtime Installation Pattern' %%| fig-width: 8.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}}%% graph TD SysPy(["System Python
owned by OS"]) OptPy(["Your Python
/opt/python/3.12.1
isolated version"]) Venv("Virtual Env
~/my-app/venv
project packages") SysPy -->|"leave untouched"| SysTools("yum, AWS CLI,
OS internal tools") OptPy -->|"create venv from"| Venv Venv -->|"install packages to"| Packages("pip install
my-packages") R(["System R
usually absent"]) OptR("Multiple R versions
/opt/R/4.6.1
/opt/R/4.3.2
rig switches") Libs("System libraries
libcurl-devel
openssl-devel
libxml2-devel") R -->|"alternative"| OptR OptR --> Libs Libs -->|"required for"| RPackages("R packages
from source") style SysPy fill:#d2562b,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff style OptPy fill:#5b8c5a,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff style Venv fill:#5b8c5a,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff style Packages fill:#2a6f77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style R fill:#d2562b,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff style OptR fill:#5b8c5a,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff style Libs fill:#e8a33d,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 style RPackages fill:#2a6f77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style SysTools fill:#2a6f77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff ``` ### Building Python from source The packaged Python is sometimes too old for what you need to run. Amazon Linux 2 ships with 3.7: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} python3 --version ``` ::: ```{.default} Python 3.7.16 ``` That's the copy `yum` depends on, so upgrading it in place is off the table. The fix is the `/opt` pattern from above: build a second Python, install it into its own versioned directory, and leave the system one alone. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Which Python Runs the App' %%| fig-width: 8.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', "fontSize":"12px"}}}}%% graph TD Check{"python3 --version
3.11 or newer?"} Yes("Use it directly") Build("Build into
/opt/python/3.12.1") Venv("/opt/myapp/.venv") Sys(["/usr/bin/python3
3.7, owned by yum"]) Check --"yes (AL2023, Ubuntu 22.04+)"--> Yes Check --"no (Amazon Linux 2)"--> Build Yes --> Venv Build --"python3 -m venv"--> Venv Sys --"leave for"--> Yum("yum, OS tooling") style Check fill:#e8a33d,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 style Yes fill:#5b8c5a,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style Build fill:#2a6f77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style Venv fill:#5b8c5a,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff,font-family:monospace style Sys fill:#d2562b,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff style Yum fill:#666,stroke:#999,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff ``` Install the compiler and the development headers first, plus a few Python needs specifically for `ssl`, `bz2`, and `ctypes` support: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo yum groupinstall -y "Development Tools" ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo yum install -y openssl-devel bzip2-devel libffi-devel zlib-devel git ``` ::: Download and unpack the source: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} cd /tmp wget https://www.python.org/ftp/python/3.12.1/Python-3.12.1.tgz tar xzf Python-3.12.1.tgz cd Python-3.12.1 ``` ::: Then configure it to land in `/opt`, and build: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo ./configure --prefix=/opt/python/3.12.1 --enable-optimizations sudo make altinstall ``` ::: `--prefix` is what keeps the install self contained. `altinstall` is the flag that matters most: it installs `python3.12` without also writing a `python3` symlink that would shadow the system copy. Confirm you got what you asked for: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} /opt/python/3.12.1/bin/python3.12 --version ``` ::: ```{.default} Python 3.12.1 ``` :::: {.callout-note collapse='true' appearance='default' icon='false'} ## [This takes a while]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.15em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.00em; color: var(--callout-body-color, #282b2d);'} `--enable-optimizations`, passed to `./configure` above, is what triples the compile time. It builds Python twice: once to produce an instrumented interpreter, then runs it against Python's own test suite to record which code paths get hit most, then rebuilds using that profile data to optimize those paths (profile guided optimization, or PGO). It also turns on link time optimization (LTO). On a `t3.micro` the whole thing takes 20 to 30 minutes with the CPU pegged. 'Runtime speed' here means how fast the finished interpreter executes Python code after it's installed, not how long the build itself takes. PGO typically buys 10 to 20 percent on CPU bound benchmarks. A subprocess-heavy or I/O-bound app isn't CPU bound, so that speedup is not something you'd notice in practice. Drop the flag (`sudo ./configure --prefix=/opt/python/3.12.1`) and the build finishes in a few minutes with a standard, unoptimized interpreter. If `make` dies partway through with an out of memory error, see [Instance Size](instance-size.qmd) for what that means and how to work around it on a small instance. More on the flag itself: ::: :::: :::: {.callout-important collapse='true' appearance='default' icon='false'} ## [pip fails with 'ssl module is not available']{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.15em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.00em; color: var(--callout-body-color, #282b2d);'} The interpreter you just built has no SSL support, so pip can't reach PyPI over HTTPS at all. The cause traces back to the `./configure` step: Amazon Linux 2's default `openssl-devel` package is OpenSSL 1.0.2k, and Python 3.10 and newer require 1.1.1 or later to build the `_ssl` extension. Configure looked for a new enough OpenSSL, didn't find one, and silently skipped the module rather than failing the build. `make altinstall` finished without complaint because none of the steps you ran so far touch SSL, so the problem doesn't show up until pip tries to talk to the internet. AL2 ships that newer OpenSSL under a separate package, `openssl11`, but its `-devel` package can't be installed alongside the old one: both own the same header path, `/usr/include/openssl/*.h`, so `yum` refuses with a conflict rather than letting them collide. The fix is to swap the devel package out, build, then swap it back, since Python only needs the headers at build time, not at runtime: > `sudo yum remove -y openssl-devel` > > `sudo yum install -y openssl11-devel` > > `cd /tmp/Python-3.12.1` > > `sudo ./configure --prefix=/opt/python/3.12.1 --enable-optimizations` > > `sudo make altinstall` Python's configure script checks for `openssl11` via `pkg-config` before falling back to the system default, which is what makes this work without a `--with-openssl` flag. You don't need to redownload the source or delete the existing `/opt/python/3.12.1` tree, `altinstall` overwrites in place. Confirm the module actually built this time before retrying the venv: `/opt/python/3.12.1/bin/python3.12 -c 'import ssl; print(ssl.OPENSSL_VERSION)'` That should print an OpenSSL 1.1.1 version string, not a traceback. Once it does, put the original devel package back so other builds on the box aren't left pointing at `openssl11`: > `sudo yum remove -y openssl11-devel` > > `sudo yum install -y openssl-devel` ::: :::: ## Installing a real application Third party software follows the same convention as the interpreter: its own directory tree under `/opt`, not scattered across the filesystem. Here's what that looks like for `baseball-trajectory`, a Shiny for Python app ([source](https://github.com/mjfrigaard/baseball-trajectory)) that plots a player's career arc from the MLB Stats API: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo git clone https://github.com/mjfrigaard/baseball-trajectory.git /opt/baseball-trajectory cd /opt/baseball-trajectory ``` ::: Create the virtual environment from the `/opt` Python, not the system one, then install the package and its dependencies into it: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo /opt/python/3.12.1/bin/python3.12 -m venv /opt/baseball-trajectory/.venv sudo /opt/baseball-trajectory/.venv/bin/pip install -e . ``` ::: This pulls the app's dependencies from PyPI, so the instance needs outbound internet access. If the box is in a private subnet, verify the NAT gateway path works before you run this rather than after it hangs. The install spreads across three locations, and each one follows the convention above rather than piling everything into one folder: | Location | What lives there | |:---------|:-----------------| | `/opt/baseball-trajectory` | Application source and the virtual environment | | `/etc/systemd/system/baseball-trajectory.service` | The unit file telling `systemd` how to run it | | `journald` | Application stdout and stderr, read with `journalctl -u baseball-trajectory` | : Where a system install of baseball-trajectory puts things {#tbl-baseball-trajectory-locations} ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'baseball-trajectory File Locations' %%| fig-width: 7.5 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', "fontSize":"12px"}}}}%% graph TD Root(["/"]) Opt("/opt/baseball-trajectory") Venv(".venv/bin/shiny
.venv/bin/baseball-trajectory") Etc("/etc/systemd/system") Unit("baseball-trajectory.service") Log("journald") Jctl("journalctl -u baseball-trajectory") Root --"application"--> Opt --> Venv Root --"config"--> Etc --> Unit Root --"logs"--> Log --> Jctl style Root fill:#d2562b,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff style Opt fill:#e8a33d,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px,color:#000,font-family:monospace style Venv fill:#e8a33d,stroke:#000,stroke-width:1px,color:#000,font-family:monospace style Etc fill:#2a6f77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff,font-family:monospace style Unit fill:#2a6f77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff,font-family:monospace style Log fill:#666,stroke:#999,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff,font-family:monospace style Jctl fill:#666,stroke:#999,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff,font-family:monospace ``` Notice what's missing: there's no `/var/lib` entry. `baseball-trajectory` keeps nothing on disk. Rosters and career stats are fetched from `https://statsapi.mlb.com` and cached in memory, so a restart simply starts with an empty cache. That also means outbound HTTPS isn't just an install time requirement; the running app needs it on every new player lookup. Before handing it to `systemd`, confirm the console script starts from the venv: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} /opt/baseball-trajectory/.venv/bin/baseball-trajectory ``` ::: It binds to `127.0.0.1:8000`, so from a second SSH session `curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8000` should return `200 OK`. See [Daemonizing with systemd](lab10.qmd) for turning this into a running service and [Linux Users](linux-users.qmd) for the dedicated account it should run as. ## Recap 1. `PATH` decides what the shell can find, and `which` tells you which copy is winning. A `command not found` error usually means a directory is missing from the list, not that the software is missing. 2. Install language runtimes into `/opt` and symlink them into `/usr/local/bin`. That keeps the system Python untouched, makes the version visible to every account and service, and turns a version change into a one line edit. 3. When the packaged interpreter is too old, build your own into `/opt` with `make altinstall` rather than touching the system copy. A real application installed the same way gets its own subtree: source and venv under `/opt`, state under `/var/lib`, unit file under `/etc/systemd/system`.
